tier_reason: First-party README charts (docs/memset_r.png, docs/memcpy_r.png, docs/memset_bench.png, docs/memcpy_bench.png) compare against glibc (via PLT and direct), musl and folly; the harness is public (src/memset/bench_memset.cc, src/memcpy/bench_memcpy.cc) and CMakeLists.txt gives -O3 -march=native -g3, but the compiler, glibc version and CPU model are never stated, so not A.

corrections.workload: README charts: (1) random-size batches, 10M calls x 20 samples (median), size and destination offset each drawn from a pre-computed random u8 sequence (0 to 255 bytes), nop-function call overhead subtracted; memset compares libc@plt, libc and asm_memset, memcpy compares libc@plt, libc, folly and asm_memcpy. (2) Hot-loop fixed-size sweeps for sizes 0 to 511 bytes (16-byte aligned buffer, 10M calls per size), memset against musl, libc@plt and libc-direct, memcpy against libc@plt, libc-direct and folly. memset always writes value 0.
corrections.hardware: Not stated (x86-64 with AVX2 required by impl.S; CPU model not given)
corrections.stars_or_usage: 344 stars, 18 forks; the memset was upstreamed into Folly as folly/memset.S (commit 0ec02d4, 2022-01-05, 'asm memset implementation' by Ilya Albrecht, citing this repo and Nadav Rotem), with folly/test/MemsetBenchmark.cpp comparing std memset and __folly_memset (no published numbers)
corrections.caveats: Results exist only as README chart images from the author's own run (values read from the images; time units not stated). CPU model, compiler and glibc version are not stated (charts date from November 2021, so glibc of that era); CMakeLists.txt uses -O3 -march=native. The repository has no LICENSE file, so its code is reference only; the Folly copy of the memset (folly/memset.S, Apache-2.0 header, AVX2-gated with a std memset fallback in FollyMemset.cpp) is the licensed route, while the memcpy was not upstreamed by that commit. The fixed-size memcpy sweep is not a uniform win: glibc direct is at or below asm_memcpy around 165 to 250 bytes (read from docs/memcpy_bench.png), and musl beats the asm memset at size 0. The random-size benchmark uses one fixed pseudo-random sequence replayed every sample. The charts predate the final memset change (2021-11-29, removal of a second exit block). Last commit 2022-01-10.

notes: Chart values match the record exactly (memset 24344/20172/14295; memcpy 28285/25263/23969/21547), so the 1.41x and 1.17x derived ratios over direct libc hold. Tier C stays: public harness and flags, but no compiler, glibc version or CPU model. Shortcomings: no license (use Folly's Apache-2.0 memset.S), author-only measurements, memcpy loses to glibc in some size ranges, abandoned since 2022.

tier_reason: Only the author's README prose gives numbers (tied with the nearest competitor, others 10.5% to 348% slower, the compiler library strstr being row 0 of the competitor list); there is no timing harness, no per-competitor table, and no compiler, flags or CPU, so first-party numbers without methodology.

corrections.baseline: The compiler's C library strstr (rows 0, 9 and 17 of Competitors/strstrFunctions.c are labelled 'Compiler library strstr'; rows 9 and 17 replaced the SunOS and Boyer-Moore-Horspool versions). The library is not named; comments in the competitor file mention macOS clang (2023-05-01), so it was probably Apple's libc, not glibc or musl.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated (competitor-file comments mention macOS clang; no flags given)
corrections.caveats: Repo holds only strstr.c and the competitor sources (Competitors/strstrFunctions.c); there is no timing harness, test corpus list, per-competitor table, CPU model, compiler or flags, so the result is not reproducible and the library strstr's own margin is never stated separately. The competitor-file header says that when the first pattern character is rare, versions that call the library's SIMD strchr (strstr7, 8, 15, 16) are about 6.5 times faster than the others (strstr1 included), so the claim holds for English-word searches and may lose to a SIMD libc strstr elsewhere. The algorithm is a naive first-character scan plus compare, O(n*m) in the worst case, unlike the linear two-way strstr in glibc and musl. The nearest competitor is GNU coreutils 5.3.0 strstr (Stephen R. van den Berg, GPL-2.0+), not current glibc. Licence: LICENSE.md says CC0 1.0 for strstr.c (no patent grant), but the file header links the Public Domain Mark URL; the Competitors file contains GPL-2.0+ and unlicensed USENET code and is not covered.

notes: README numbers quoted correctly; the competitor file confirms strstr1 and strstr20 (GNU coreutils 5.3.0) within 0.5% on English and French text. Tier C stays, low confidence: no harness or methodology, unnamed libc (probably macOS), naive worst-case algorithm, 3 stars. Metadata checked: CC0-1.0 via LICENSE.md, last commit 2026-06-21, active.

tier_reason: The only numbers are one comment by the code's contributor in issue #580, measured on his own go-sqlite3 SIMD libc under wazero via a GitHub Actions run, with no CPU, runtime version, compiler, flags or string sizes; first-party without methodology, so C. Downgraded for scope: three of the ten listed routines are not SIMD in wasi-libc at all.

corrections.claimed_speedup: ncruces, issue #580 (May 9, 2025), 'Numbers are rough, and only for wazero': memchr 4.3x, memcmp 10.0x, strlen 4.9x, strchr 4.2x, strrchr 9.9x, strcmp 12.8x, strncmp 16.3x, strspn 9.1x, strcspn 9.7x, strstr 5.6x, geomean 7.8x over musl's SWAR versions. These were measured on ncruces's go-sqlite3 libc (sqlite3/libc/string.h), not on a wasi-libc build. wasi-libc main has opt-in SIMD versions only of strlen (#586), memchr (#592), strchrnul and hence strchr (#594), memrchr and hence strrchr (#598), memcmp (#603) and strspn/strcspn (#597); strcmp, strncmp and strstr are still the scalar musl code, so the 12.8x, 16.3x and 5.6x figures do not apply to wasi-libc. July 2, 2025: with the #586 strlen gist changed to 10-byte strings, 'the improvement (using wasmtime on amd64) is still around 2x'.
corrections.workload: Per-function speedup of wasm simd128 string.h routines over musl's scalar SWAR code, run from Go under the wazero runtime (go-sqlite3 GitHub Actions run 14516931864, x86-64 and AArch64), string sizes not stated (a reviewer asked whether a 4 MB string from libc_test.go was used); plus strlen on 10-byte strings under wasmtime on amd64.
corrections.hardware: Not stated for the table (issue cites x86-64 and AArch64 GitHub Actions runners under wazero; the 10-byte strlen run was wasmtime on amd64). In PR #592 ncruces measured with wasmtime on a Xeon W-2135 and found the any_true versus bitmask difference 'hard to measure'.
corrections.caveats: Numbers are one rough comment in a tracking issue, measured on the contributor's go-sqlite3 implementations rather than the code later merged into wasi-libc, with no CPU, runtime version, compiler, flags or string sizes; a reviewer asked whether the table used a 4 MB string and the reply gave no size, only saying small calls are hard to measure from the host and that 'there are too many variables (Wasm runtime, CPU architecture, string length), to give any hard guarantees'. Only strlen, memchr, strchr, strrchr, memcmp, strspn and strcspn have SIMD paths in wasi-libc; strcmp, strncmp and strstr stay scalar. The SIMD routines are off by default (-DSIMD=ON, __wasilibc_simd_string), and strspn/strcspn SIMD is skipped on Clang 19 and 20 (llvm/llvm-project#146574 ICE). The baseline is wasm-to-wasm (scalar vs SIMD in the same libc), not native glibc. The go-sqlite3 libc README with updated numbers linked from the issue now returns 404.

notes: Issue #580 table matches the record, but it measures ncruces's go-sqlite3 libc; wasi-libc main (checked in libc-top-half/musl/src/string) merged SIMD only for strlen, memchr, strchrnul, memrchr, memcmp and strspn/strcspn, so strcmp/strncmp/strstr claims are dropped from scope. Tier stays C. Metadata confirmed: ~1.0k stars, 255 forks, last commit 2026-10-01, Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception / Apache-2.0 / MIT, active.
